findings.suggested_fix: Integrate `MATCHING/fs_avg_performance.do` into a documented top-level workflow (such as `replication/run_machineA.do` or a dedicated FamilySearch batch driver). Add `link1930_1940_fs*.dta` and the divided-file directories to preflight checks, and ensure path resolution does not fail across environments.
findings.title: No documented master workflow runs or preflights the new scorer
findings.what_the_code_does: `fs_avg_performance.do` alone reads all five link variants and writes `MATCHING/results/fs_avg_performance.tex`. Neither documented entry point (`replication/run_machineA.do` / `Run-MachineA.ps1` or `MATCHING/_matching_master_dofile.do`) executes or preflights this script or its FamilySearch inputs. `_matching_master_dofile.do` exits after appending links for a single requested run, while `run_machineA.do` preflights only Ancestry and ML links, omitting the three `link1930_1940_fs*.dta` inputs and divided-file directories. In addition, line 23 hardcodes `D:/repos/fixing_transcription_errors/replication/config.do`, and `config.do` does not define `REP_SNU` or `REP_F` for Machine B.
findings.why_it_matters: Following either documented entry point will not reproduce the new FamilySearch comparison table. Missing or corrupted FamilySearch link files also bypass preflight verification, allowing submitted results to rely on undocumented manual execution or outdated intermediates.

findings.how_to_check: Inspect the generated `MATCHING/results/fs_avg_performance.tex`. Note that lines 158-160 are LaTeX comments that do not compile into document text. Note the discrepancy between `sva_target_ans` and `sv_target_ans` reported in the console at line 142.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an explicit, visible table note or footnote within the exported LaTeX table environment explaining the provenance of middle initials in each row and column, and documenting why Ancestry's validation rate differs between Row 3 and Row 5.
findings.title: Validation rows mix different middle-initial extraction sources across columns and produce contradictory Ancestry validation rates without visible explanation
findings.what_the_code_does: In line 89, `val_\`c\'' evaluates `mi1930==mi1940` using link-file initials: Ancestry links use `matching_intgen` initials, ML links use 1930 `matching_intgen` and 1940 ML initials, and FamilySearch links use divided-file initials (FS where available, Ancestry fallback). In line 96, `valanc_\`c\'' rescores all links using divided-file Ancestry initials. Because `matching_intgen` and divided-file Ancestry initials differ, Ancestry's own validation rate differs between Row 3 ('Share validated (%)') and Row 5 ('Share validated, Ancestry initials (%)'), as trapped at line 141. The script writes explanations only as LaTeX percent comments (`% Own initials...`) at lines 158-160, which are discarded during LaTeX compilation and never rendered in the document.
findings.why_it_matters: Row 3 conflates linkage accuracy with differences in initial extraction across sources. Furthermore, presenting two different validation rates for Ancestry in Row 3 and Row 5 side by side with no visible footnote or explanation creates the direct appearance of an internal contradiction or calculation bug to readers and referees.

findings.how_to_check: Compute the baseline share of records with non-empty FamilySearch names in the candidate divided files / 1940 labeled data, and compare it with the linked shares reported at lines 120-121.
findings.suggested_fix: Report the baseline FamilySearch availability/substitution rate in the candidate target and all-records populations as additional rows in the table alongside the existing conditional-on-linkage rows.
findings.title: FamilySearch name usage rates are reported only conditional on linkage, concealing baseline availability in the target population
findings.what_the_code_does: In lines 90-93, `fs\`y\'_\`c\'' is generated with `if linked_\`c\'==1`, leaving unlinked records as missing (`.`). Lines 120-121 summarize `fs\`y\'_\`c\'`, so the exported mean reflects FamilySearch usage strictly among records that successfully linked. The table at lines 173-184 reports 'Links with an FS name in <year> (%)', but does not report the baseline availability of FamilySearch names in the candidate or target population.
findings.why_it_matters: Because the FamilySearch specifications represent a hybrid rule falling back field by field to Ancestry when FamilySearch names are blank, differences in linkage rates reflect both transcription quality and selective substitution into the candidate pool. Conditioning exposure solely on successful linkage conceals whether differential linkage performance is driven by transcription quality or differential availability across subgroups.

review_limits: No paper draft was supplied (per prompt instructions); claims-vs-code review was evaluated against code comments, table headers, and generated LaTeX outputs rather than manuscript prose.

The external census, divided-file, and intermediate link datasets were unavailable in the repository, and the Stata pipeline could not be executed; numerical results and merge outcomes were inferred via static code inspection.
The review was scoped to uncommitted working-tree changes (MATCHING/fs_avg_performance.do) and directly relevant upstream matching scripts.
summary: The updated FamilySearch performance scorer resolves the previous runtime crash on asymmetric indicator variables and maintains strict replication gates verifying Ancestry and ML baseline statistics against published paper values. However, the script remains omitted from master replication workflows and preflight checks, while the generated LaTeX table presents conflicting Ancestry validation rates without visible explanatory notes and conditions FamilySearch exposure solely on linkage.
